query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The peculiar stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior of the HfNbTaTiZr refractory HEA is primarily governed by the interaction between residual dislocation networks (introduced during cold rolling and partially preserved during aging) and locally generated thermal stresses that arise from non‐uniform thermal expansion, which modulate dislocation activation and recovery processes during deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: A cold-rolled, single-phase BCC HfNbTaTiZr alloy possessing a heterogeneous distribution of residual dislocation structures and slight local variations in lattice parameters due to atomic size/misfit effects.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of samples: one set processed by cold rolling (thus retaining residual dislocations and thermal expansion mismatch stress fields) and a second set that is annealed to largely remove the dislocation networks and homogenize the thermal strain fields. Then, subject both sets to a range of mechanical tests (tensile, creep, and elastic modulus measurements) over the temperature range from room temperature (~293 K) up to 1250 °C.
generation.conditions: Testing under a controlled atmosphere with well‐calibrated strain rates and isothermal holds; temperature range from room temperature (293 K) to high temperature (1250 °C); and a comparison between cold-worked versus annealed (dislocation‐reduced) states.
generation.structural_mediator: Residual dislocation networks and local lattice strain heterogeneities arising from thermal expansion mismatch at the microstructural scale that act together as internal stress fields.
generation.mechanism: During deformation, the stored residual dislocations in the cold-rolled alloy enhance work hardening by increasing resistance to further dislocation motion. Simultaneously, nonuniform thermal expansion creates local residual stresses that either aid or oppose the applied stress depending on their orientation. At intermediate temperatures (600–800 °C), these internal thermal stresses reinforce the activation barrier for dislocation glide, while at very high temperatures (around 1250 °C) enhanced thermal activation permits dynamic recovery and partial annihilation of dislocations, leading to creep softening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the annealed (homogenized) samples, cold-rolled specimens will exhibit a higher initial yield strength accompanied by a pronounced work hardening region at temperatures below ~800 °C. However, at temperatures approaching 1250 °C, the cold-rolled samples will show a more significant reduction in strength (creep softening) due to thermally activated dynamic recovery. The baseline annealed samples, with fewer residual dislocations and less local thermal stress, should display more conventional, less anomalous thermoelastic behavior.
generation.baseline: Samples processed to eliminate or substantially reduce residual dislocation density (through high-temperature annealing) with minimal local thermal expansion mismatch effects.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be most influential in the temperature regime where thermal expansion differences can build appreciable local stresses (roughly 600–800 °C) and where dislocation mobility is still limited by obstacles (up to about 1250 °C). Outside this range (e.g., at room temperature or deep in the fully softened high-temperature regime), other mechanisms may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: While the interplay between residual dislocations and thermal expansion induced stresses is supported by separate observations of work hardening (in cold rolled and aged alloys) and temperature-dependent elastic behavior, the quantitative contributions of thermal mismatch versus dislocation network evolution remain uncertain and may be influenced by slight chemical segregations or secondary phase formations not fully ruled out.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of HfNbTaTiZr samples: one group retains cold rolling induced dislocation structures (and thus thermal mismatch fields) while the other group is fully annealed to remove these features. Subject both groups to identical tensile creep and elastic modulus tests over a controlled temperature range (293 K to 1250 °C). Additionally, use in situ techniques (e.g., TEM or neutron diffraction) to monitor dislocation density and local lattice strains during deformation.
measurements: Yield strength and work hardening rate as functions of temperature
Creep rate and flow stress at high temperature
In situ dislocation density and lattice strain mapping (via TEM/neutron diffraction)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the cold-rolled and annealed samples exhibit nearly identical stress–strain behavior and temperature-dependent elastic moduli (i.e., similar work hardening, yield strength, and creep softening) despite the marked differences in dislocation density and expected thermal mismatch fields, then the hypothesis that the residual dislocation networks coupled with thermal expansion mismatch govern the anomalous behavior would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The differentials between the UTS and YS were about 100 MPa, and gradually widened as the temperature rose. Work hardening appeared in all curves from RT to 1073 K. We speculated that this was due to the fact that the heat treatment did not completely eliminate the residual stress of the alloy after cold rolling [,]. In order to prove this, the rolled samples were analyzed by transmission electron microscopy before a tensile test (see Figure 5). Some obvious dense dislocation bands were found in Figure 5a, and in addition, the diffraction pattern indicated that the alloy retained the structure of a single-phase BCC after the prior treatment. The region where the dislocation band was located was enlarged to further analyze its composition. In Figure 5b, it can be clearly found that the previously thought dislocation band was composed of two rows of dislocations. After a further enlargement, it was found that each dislocation band was composed of dense, short dislocations. This proved the previous conjecture that the residual dislocation after cold rolling caused a work hardening of the alloy.

Our first attempt in research of HEAs was therefore related to HfNbTaTiZr refractory metal alloy []. Our research was inspired by Senkov [] and confirmed our expectations. Ingots produced by vacuum arc melting possessed single phase solid solution microstructure, with a high room temperature tensile strength and ductility. Some of the elements used in the HfNbTaTiZr alloy are very similar to each other with very similar chemical behaviour; Nb is chemically similar to Ta and Zr to Hf. Therefore a question has emerged whether it is necessary to use all of these elements in order to get random solid solution and good mechanical properties (high strength and sufficient ductility). The design of the present experiment was as follows. First, we reduced the original HfNbTaTiZr alloy system by removing Hf, which is almost identical to Zr from the chemical point of view, then we distracted Ta, which is very similar to Nb; thus getting NbTiZr alloy with equiatomic concentrations. Then we produced also other 3 element combinations containing Ti, namely TaTiZr and NbTaTi. Investigations of mechanical properties and microstructure of different MEAs derived from the HfNbTaTiZr alloy system has been performed. It has been shown that ductility is significantly reduced by simultaneous presence of Ta and Zr in the alloy, which leads to reduction of the BCC1 phase content. These elements segregate during solidifying. Because of the miscibility gap in the Ta-Zr equilibrium phase diagram two BCC phases are found after cooling to room temperature. Clear correlation between the BCC1 phase content and the total elongation to failure of the alloy was found. Precipitation of Ta rich precipitates on grain boundaries reduces the elongation to almost zero values. No correlation was found between the tensile mechanical properties and microstructure related parameters in investigated set of alloys. The 5 element HEA alloy exhibits the best combination of strength and elongation. 4 and 3 element MEAs have lower strength to various extent. Some of them are ductile (NbTaTiZr, NbTaTi, NbTiZr) but some of them are brittle (TaTiZr, Nb1.5TaTiZr0.5, Nb0.5TaTiZr1.5) depending on microstructure.
